items.title: 1. Call Medics For and the lines after it: insomnia, "acting delusional", and naloxone
items.question:
a) "Severe insomnia" came into this list from your paragraph in round 35 ("my paragraph should not say anything that should be going in that above list"). There it was a reason to reach out; here it calls an ambulance, and a night without sleep is usual after MDMA or a trip, so readers took it for a sign they'd always see. Did you mean days without sleep? Then it would read "No sleep for days", or it could go back to reaching out.
b) "Another cue to get help is if they start acting delusional." Most bad trips bring delusions, so readers took it as "always get help". Did you mean acting on one (heading out the door because of it, as in the sentence before)?
c) The guide never names naloxone. Fentanyl has turned up in pills sold as MDMA ([14 of 22 samples at one festival](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10698886/)), and naloxone, sold over the counter in the US, reverses an opioid overdose ([CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/stop-overdose/naloxone-faq/)); it does nothing to someone without opioids in them and wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, sooner than some opioids ([Jed Foundation](https://jedfoundation.org/resource/naloxone-101-how-to-use-it-to-save-lives-from-opioid-overdose/)). Mine, as a paragraph after this list (quiz 2, card 3, scores my reading of it):
"Slow, shallow breathing can mean an opioid overdose, which naloxone reverses, so if you have it (the Narcan nasal spray), spray it into one nostril right away. It doesn't matter if they think they only took MDMA, since fentanyl, an opioid, has turned up in pills sold as MDMA, and naloxone does no harm without one. But naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so call medics even if they wake up, and if their breathing slows again before help comes, give the second spray in the pack."
In, or not?

items.title: 2. Swallowed Too Much?: slow breathing, or a slow heartbeat, with iboga?
items.question: "Slow breathing is normal with iboga, but if cardiac irregularities come along with it, that's an extra danger sign." Ibogaine is known to slow the heart, not the breathing: in [a 2022 study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9292417/) it lowered heart rate and blood pressure, and the deaths linked to it come from heart rhythm problems ([review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26807959/)). I found nothing on slow breathing. Did you mean "A slow heartbeat is normal with iboga, but if it comes with an irregular one, that's an extra danger sign"? Or is slow breathing something you have seen with it?
items.comment:
gpt says: Yes. Slower breathing is a recognized effect of iboga/ibogaine, and people do report experiencing it. However, the evidence does not establish that clinically significant respiratory depression is a common effect.

Here's what I found:

1. Ibogaine Safety Guidelines: The clinical guidelines explicitly list slowed breathing among ibogaine's physiological effects, alongside slowed heart rate, nausea, tremor, and changes in blood pressure. 
IBOGAINE SAFETY GUIDELINES


2. Firsthand experience: A 2015 Erowid report describes breathing becoming progressively slower and subtler during iboga meditation, sometimes followed by a sudden deep inhalation. 
'Self Inquiry and Resetting'


3. Clinical research: A 2018 analysis of 191 medically monitored ibogaine recipients found respiratory rates generally remained unremarkable, with only minor changes from baseline at doses of approximately 8–12 mg/kg. This suggests substantial respiratory slowing is not inevitable. 
pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov


4. More concerning reports: One Reddit user described apparently stopping breathing briefly, then gasping, accompanied by heart palpitations during an iboga ceremony. In a documented 2019 medical case, a woman experienced apnea (temporary cessation of breathing), seizures, and dangerous cardiac arrhythmias after ingesting ibogaine. 
reddit.com+1

What this means
Three possibilities need distinguishing:
- Slower, comfortable breathing: Possibly associated with relaxation or altered awareness, without impaired ventilation.
- Respiratory depression: Breathing becomes too slow or shallow to adequately remove carbon dioxide and maintain oxygenation.
- Breathing pauses associated with cardiac or neurological complications: Potentially dangerous even when someone does not initially appear distressed.

items.title: 3. Quiz 2, no Pangram: my reading of my new lines on this page
items.question:
These are the lines I wrote for this page: the dose in step 2, step 6 as I'd pick it (card 4), the seizure in step 7 (card 5) and the naloxone paragraph (card 1). Three fresh readers read them once and I answered their marks; Pangram hasn't seen them, on purpose. Under each is my reading. Score each reading right or wrong ("S3 wrong: ..."), and name any sentence I read as right that you'd mark.
Step 2
S1: "If you do get it, I'd give an adult 12 mg to start, and tell the medics you did."
My reading: not sure, "If you do get it" ties it to the line before and the dose comes at once, but "to start" leaves the next doses unsaid (I left those to the medics, since the ambulance comes long before two hours).

Step 6
S2: "If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from MDMA: Magnesium Alarm above, they may need a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more salt and magnesium than a normal one."
My reading: reads right, "still" ties it to the sips, and the drink, in your bold, comes as soon as the condition is said; the signs stay in your MDMA section, as you asked, so the reader follows the link.
S3: "That can be as simple as a pinch of salt and some magnesium chloride flakes stirred into an ordinary one, or a salty broth with the flakes in it."
My reading: not sure, your "as simple as" and what a kitchen has, but "some" flakes is no amount, and the amounts your MDMA section gives are for jaw tension, not a drink.
S4: "And while you might think to add potassium too, since it can run low after MDMA, I wouldn't add any, because muscles breaking down into the blood release a lot of it, and too much can stop the heart."
My reading: not sure, your "And while you might think" names the urge before the don't, and the reason comes from step 5, but it carries two reasons (since, because) and may be one too many.

Step 7
S5: "And if they have a seizure while you wait, do the first aid in Active Seizure above."
My reading: reads right, "while you wait" ties it to the step, and it points to your first aid instead of saying it again.
S6: "Then I'd tell the medics whether their breathing got better or worse afterward, since the CDC counts trouble breathing after a seizure as a danger sign."
My reading: reads right, your act and your reason in your order ("make note if their breathing is getting better or worse"), with the seizure now one they had and who the note is for.

After Call Medics For
S7: "Slow, shallow breathing can mean an opioid overdose, which naloxone reverses, so if you have it (the Narcan nasal spray), spray it into one nostril right away."
My reading: not sure, the reason first, as in your steps, but three things come before the act (what it may be, what reverses it, the brand in brackets).
S8: "It doesn't matter if they think they only took MDMA, since fentanyl, an opioid, has turned up in pills sold as MDMA, and naloxone does no harm without one."
My reading: reads right, your "It doesn't matter if" answers the doubt the reader will have, then both reasons to give it anyway.
S9: "But naloxone can wear off before the opioid does, so call medics even if they wake up, and if their breathing slows again before help comes, give the second spray in the pack."
My reading: not sure, "But" ties it, and each act follows from the wearing off, but two acts in one sentence, the second with its own condition.

**The most useful clues are how much water the person drank, whether they seem bloated or have gained weight, and whether they are developing neurological symptoms.** Sweating and dancing are not reliable indicators of low sodium. Thirst tends to favor dehydration in endurance athletes, but MDMA itself causes dry mouth and thirst, making that clue less reliable.

I checked the previous PDF: page 6 briefly mentions oral sodium, but page 4 focuses on IV treatment. The guide needs a different decision pathway for a festival with no medical equipment.

## **How to distinguish the two problems**

| Clue                                                        | What it suggests                                                  |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Drank large amounts of water relative to activity           | Favors dilutional hyponatremia                                    |
| Bloating, puffy hands, tight rings, or weight gain          | Favors water retention and possible hyponatremia                  |
| Little water intake after prolonged exertion in heat        | Favors dehydration                                                |
| Genuine thirst, dizziness on standing, dry mucous membranes | Favors dehydration, but less reliable after MDMA                  |
| Heavy sweating, dancing, fast heartbeat                     | Cannot distinguish them                                           |
| Headache, nausea, vomiting, muscle cramps                   | Can occur with either                                             |
| Confusion, difficulty walking normally, seizures, collapse  | Medical emergency; cannot determine the cause from symptoms alone |

This distinction comes from the Wilderness Medical Society 2019 exercise-associated hyponatremia guideline, published in 2020. Its clinical assessment emphasizes fluid-intake history, signs of excess water retention, and signs of volume depletion. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://journals.sagepub.com\&sz=32)

journals.sagepub.com+1



Importantly, the 2024 controlled MDMA research found that MDMA itself increases thirst and can impair water excretion. Therefore, the endurance-athlete clues do not transfer perfectly to MDMA exposure. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://jamanetwork.com\&sz=32)

jamanetwork.com



## **So when would oral sodium make sense?**

1

**Fully alert, mild symptoms, and a convincing history of overhydration**

This is the situation in which the Wilderness Medical Society recommends restricting further fluids and permits sodium-rich food or concentrated salty broth if the person is neurologically intact, swallowing normally, and minimally nauseated.

The guideline actually describes a concentrated broth example containing 3–4 bouillon cubes, each supplying approximately 880 mg sodium, in 125 mL water. This is a recommendation for **mild suspected exercise-associated hyponatremia**, not a validated MDMA treatment or a general salt-soup recipe. Cube sodium contents vary. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://journals.sagepub.com\&sz=32)

journals.sagepub.com



2

**Fully alert, with signs favoring dehydration rather than water retention**

Cooling, rest, and small sips of appropriately mixed oral rehydration solution are more appropriate than concentrated salt. Avoid forcing large fluid volumes, particularly after MDMA.

3

**Confusion, seizures, major deterioration, or unsafe swallowing**

This is not a situation for oral sodium, soup, or Epsom salt. Even if dangerously low sodium is the cause, **oral salt is not a reliable substitute for emergency IV hypertonic saline** and may cause choking or aspiration.

Activate emergency evacuation immediately, protect breathing and the person during seizures, and start external cooling if overheating is suspected. Severe low sodium, heatstroke, and serotonin toxicity may coexist. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://journals.sagepub.com\&sz=32)

journals.sagepub.com+1



The key distinction is **mild suspected hyponatremia in someone neurologically intact versus severe neurological illness**. The WMS recommendation for oral sodium does not establish that concentrated salt is effective or safe for a confused person after MDMA. Suspected mild cases still need close observation and medical assessment, because symptoms can progress.

I've made a separate one-page decision aid for this low-resource situation.

**Festival MDMA: When to Give Oral Sodium**

One-page PDF · No medications, IVs, or blood tests · Evidence-qualified field guide

Open the decision guide

The original ten-page clinician guide remains unchanged. This is a standalone, more relevant addendum.

**What I checked:** The existing PDF, the full 2019 Wilderness Medical Society field-treatment guidance, the 2024 controlled MDMA fluid study, and current MDMA clinical references.

**Not established:** A validated symptom-only rule for deciding that an MDMA-exposed person needs sodium, or a safe and effective oral sodium rescue regimen for severe MDMA-associated hyponatremia.

The remaining research question is whether direct MDMA case reports or field experience establish an oral intervention when IV treatment cannot be reached. The exercise-associated guidance alone cannot answer that.

Next step: Use the one-page guide as a provisional aid for discussion with festival medical organizers, not as an approved standing order.

items.title: 4. Step 6: your hypertonic drink in bold, and two things in it
items.question:
Your answer (b): "a hypertonic drink could be as simple as throwing in a bit extra salt, potassium and magnesium, or even just a salty potato soup with some epsom salt thrown in", with the bold you asked for. The signs it is for are in your MDMA: Magnesium Alarm (confusion or headache that worsens, vomiting that won't stop, muscles getting weaker), so step 6 points there instead of saying them again. Two things in it I'd change, and one I'd leave:
a) Potassium. Serotonin syndrome can break muscle down into the blood (your step 5), broken muscle releases potassium, and too much of it can stop the heart ([StatPearls](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448168/), [a review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19046720/)). It can also run low after MDMA, as your MDMA section says, and only a blood test tells which. I'd add none and leave it to the ER.
b) Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, the laxative kind your MDMA section steers away from ("less likely to cause diarrhea than ... forms deliberately used as laxatives"), and diarrhea dries them out more. Potatoes are also high in potassium. I'd use your magnesium chloride flakes, in broth.
c) Magnesium is then in step 6's drink and in step 8; the drink's is a little, so I'd leave both.

1) As you put it:
"Overstimulating also dehydrates them, but we can't give fluids unless they're fully alert, able to swallow and not vomiting, and then just small sips of an electrolyte drink. If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from [MDMA: Magnesium Alarm](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/170920118/mdma-magnesium-alarm) above, they may need **a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more magnesium and potassium than a normal one**. That can be as simple as an ordinary one with a bit of each thrown in, plus extra salt, or even a salty potato soup with some Epsom salt."

2) Mine, without potassium or Epsom salt (quiz 2, S2 to S4):
"Overstimulating also dehydrates them, but we can't give fluids unless they're fully alert, able to swallow and not vomiting, and then just small sips of an electrolyte drink. If they still show the signs of low electrolytes from [MDMA: Magnesium Alarm](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/i/170920118/mdma-magnesium-alarm) above, they may need **a hypertonic electrolyte drink with more salt and magnesium than a normal one**. That can be as simple as a pinch of salt and some magnesium chloride flakes stirred into an ordinary one, or a salty broth with the flakes in it. And while you might think to add potassium too, since it can run low after MDMA, I wouldn't add any, because muscles breaking down into the blood release a lot of it, and too much can stop the heart."

items.title: 5. The serotonin steps: what readers still couldn't tell
items.question:
a) Step 7: "Keep track of how their breathing is doing, as that's one of the main indicators of how dangerous the seizure is" comes before any seizure in the steps, so readers took "the seizure" for one they'd missed. Mine (quiz 2, S5 and S6): "And if they have a seizure while you wait, do the first aid in Active Seizure above. Then I'd tell the medics whether their breathing got better or worse afterward, since the CDC counts trouble breathing after a seizure as a danger sign." Or just "a seizure, if they have one".
b) Step 2, the dose. The Maryland Poison Center's adult dose is 12 mg, then 2 mg every two hours while the symptoms last, up to 32 mg a day ([their sheet](https://www.mdpoison.com/media/SOP/mdpoisoncom/healthcareprofessionals/antidote-facts/Cyproheptadine%20Antidote%20Facts.pdf)). The ambulance comes long before a second dose, so mine gives the first only (quiz 2, S1). In, or leave dosing to whoever prescribes it?
c) Step 8 gives niacin's reason for "I wouldn't use either one here", but not DMSO's. What's the reason for DMSO? (The guide before said only "DMSO is also not part of this branch.")
d) Step 8, the oil: readers stop at "almost none of the harmala alkaloids" followed by "could help or harm": if there's almost none, what could harm? Your answer was "potentially helpful, potentially harmful with mdma", and if used, cautiously, raising the dose slowly. Say what could harm (a trace of an MAOI with MDMA?), or put it your way: "if you use it, start with a little and go up slowly"?
e) Step 5: "fidgeting (especially of the calf muscle, flexing the feet)". Flexing the foot up is how doctors set off clonus, the muscle jerking in your Hunter list ([Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine](https://www.ccjm.org/content/83/11/810)), and every jerk makes heat. Keep the feet, or fidgeting with the hands?

**Yes. I found several firsthand reports of DMSO being used for seizures**, including one human account and two animal accounts reporting improvement.

### **Reports found**

1\. **Human seizures — improvement over one year (2026).** A reader of *The Forgotten Side of Medicine* reported using DMSO for a year and no longer needing emergency visits every three days for seizures. The report does not specify the dose, route, or other treatments. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.midwesterndoctor.com\&sz=32)

midwesterndoctor.com



2\. **Dog with recurring seizures — reported cessation (November 2025).** A commenter named Diane Weber described treating her elderly dog with topical DMSO and castor oil, later adding oral DMSO. She reported that seizures stopped and the dog improved within hours, although it also had several other serious conditions. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.coffeeandcovid.com\&sz=32)

coffeeandcovid.com



3\. **Cat with epilepsy — reported seizure freedom.** A reader of *Healing with DMSO* described replacing the cat's long-term anticonvulsant medication with DMSO and reported no subsequent seizures. The report does not establish how long the cat was followed. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://yummy.doctor\&sz=32)

Holistic Health Education



These are testimonials rather than controlled observations. The dog and cat reports concern animals, and none demonstrates that DMSO can reliably stop an active seizure.

### **Additional findings**

- **Earth Clinic forum (2016):** One commenter recommended topical DMSO for a teenager experiencing seizures after head injuries, but he was repeating something he'd read, not reporting a successful treatment. 

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://www.earthclinic.com\&sz=32)

  earthclinic.com

- **1970 US patent:** Stanley Jacob and Robert Herschler described two men with epilepsy treated using DMSO. One reported no seizures for a month; the second reportedly had no convulsions during treatment and an improved EEG after seven weeks. These were uncontrolled case descriptions in a patent, not clinical trial results. 

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com\&sz=32)

  patentimages.storage.googleapis.com

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://patentimages.storage.googleapis.com\&sz=32)

  patentimages.storage.googleapis.com

- **1988 clinical case report:** An eight-year-old girl with Niemann–Pick disease type C experienced fewer seizures and improved EEG findings during two years of oral DMSO treatment, despite a reduction in one anticonvulsant. 

  [image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://openalex.org\&sz=32)

  openalex.org



### **What about using DMSO to stop an active seizure?**

**I did not find a clear, firsthand human forum account demonstrating that applying DMSO during an ongoing seizure stopped it.** The positive accounts mostly concern reducing recurrent seizures.

The experimental evidence is mixed. DMSO temporarily reduced epileptic activity in one 2023 mouse study, while other research found increased seizure-like activity under certain conditions. Seizures have also occurred during DMSO-containing stem-cell infusions. 

[image](https://www.google.com/s2/favicons?domain=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov\&sz=32)

pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov+2



So there is a research lead worth investigating, but DMSO is not an established seizure-rescue treatment. During an active convulsive seizure, it should not replace prescribed rescue medication or emergency care, particularly if the seizure lasts five minutes or longer.
